title: New England Governors Ask Congress for $3B More in Home Heating Aid This Winter - Boston's ROCK 92.9

 Local News New England Governors Ask Congress for $3B More in Home Heating Aid This Winter
 As colder temperatures settle in across New England, the governors of all six New England states are asking Congress to add $3 billion to the Low Income Home Energy Assistance…
 Michael Vyskocil 
 Published Nov 12, 2026 5:33 AM EST Share this story As colder temperatures settle in across New England, the governors of all six New England states are asking Congress to add $3 billion to the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), bringing total funding to $7 billion as households face steep heating costs this winter.
 Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont, Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee, Maine Gov. Janet Mills, New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte, and Vermont Gov. Phil Scott signed the letter. These governors addressed their letter to House Appropriations Chair Tom Cole and Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins.
 “I am deeply concerned about how my seniors, how my families are going to stay warm,” said Executive Councilor Janet Stevens  in a statement shared with WMUR News 9 . “I have retired principals going back to teaching at a substitute level because they're concerned about filling up their tanks.”
 The governors cite projections from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association that heating oil prices will rise about 50% this winter. That leaves low-income Northeastern households facing nearly $1.1 billion in additional heating-oil costs. New England is especially exposed because of cold winters, older housing, and reliance on delivered fuel.
 The pressure on households is already evident in Maine , where heating oil serves about half of homes and averaged a record $6.04 per gallon in October .
 In Massachusetts, home heating oil averaged $5.94 per gallon on Nov. 9, more than $2 above its $3.74 average a year earlier, despite a 3.73% decline from the previous week, according to a WBUR report .
 WBUR further noted that Massachusetts received $142.3 million in LIHEAP funding this year, nearly $4 million less than its initial allocation last year after a five-year increase under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law expired. Only 20% of eligible households receive assistance annually, according to Congresswoman Lori Trahan's office.
 In their letter, the governors warn that rising prices will erode LIHEAP's purchasing power, potentially forcing states to reduce benefits or help fewer eligible households. 
 "While our states are working to mitigate the immediate impact of rising energy costs on vulnerable households and continue to invest heavily in energy efficiency, weatherization, and other long-term solutions, these efforts cannot fully offset the immediate financial pressures facing families this winter," the governors wrote.
